video_title: Why Oil Could Still Go Much Higher with Josh Young, Bison Interests | The Geopolitical Edge
gist: Bison Interests' Josh Young argues oil sits near $100 rather than $200 because of US sanction waivers, a stock-flow mini glut and overt price-suppression jawboning, while inventories are down over a billion barrels and the US-Iran war likely continues. He expects record refining cracks to mean-revert toward crude, is hedged with 'TACO insurance' puts and small shorts on refiners and tankers, and favors small-cap producers and onshore services; he avoids nat gas due to trader-driven oversupply.

themes.theme: Why oil is ~$100, not $200: price suppression and stock-flow glut

insights.claim: Forecasts of $200 Brent by the midterms failed because they assumed restricted Gulf flows would stay restricted and that the US would prosecute the Iran war rationally; instead the US fully waived sanctions on Iranian oil around May-June, releasing a wave of long-stored Iranian and other Persian Gulf barrels.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: The sub-$200 outcome reflects policy choices (sanction waivers), not loose fundamentals.

insights.claim: Global oil inventories appear to be down more than one billion barrels since the start of 2026, yet a June wave of released barrels created a 'mini glut in the middle of a larger shortage' - a stock-flow problem that let prices fall while inventories kept dropping.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Low inventories plus temporarily soft prices set up an asymmetric upside once the flow wave passes.
insights.quote: having sort of a mini glut in the middle of a larger shortage sort of a stock flow type problem

insights.claim: Trump and senior US officials have said the Iran war is ending soon or already won over a hundred times, and the big peace announcements have landed exactly when oil charts were breaking out, which Young reads as overt price suppression - and historically such government suppression ends in much higher prices.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Jawboning is losing effectiveness; Young treats it as a bullish signal rather than a bearish one.
insights.quote: that looks a lot to me like overt price suppression

insights.claim: US inventories are down roughly 300-400 million barrels of crude plus 100 million-plus barrels of products, with diesel at five-year seasonal lows and diesel prices near $250 per barrel, and gasoline and jet fuel stocks also very low.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Product tightness in the US is acute and supports high cracks and pump prices.
insights.quote: we're at last I checked fiveyear seasonal lows for diesel which is partly why diesel prices are close to $250 a barrel

insights.claim: US SPR releases have dropped to under half a million barrels a week from a peak near 10 million barrels a week, a twentieth or less of the peak, possibly because easily accessible uncontaminated barrels are running out - while Trump pushes Europe to release its own stocks.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: If SPR releases capped prices, their exhaustion or refill should remove a price lid.

themes.theme: Hormuz, tanker attacks and the information war

insights.claim: Despite US claims, the US has not won the battle of Hormuz: officials (including Energy Secretary Chris Wright) touted flows about a month before they showed in physical data, and flows exceeded pre-war levels for only two or three days before Iran stepped up tanker attacks.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Headlines about restored Hormuz flows are unreliable and short-lived.

insights.claim: The UK Maritime authority confirmed a batch of tanker hits as 'late reports' about a week and a half after an IRGC-linked outlet claimed 19 tankers attacked, and Young argues withholding confirmation induced more tankers, backed by US insurance, to transit.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Delayed attack confirmation inflated transit volumes that are now likely to reverse.

insights.claim: Peak tanker flows through Hormuz are likely behind us for a while: tankers have reportedly turned around after IRGC threats, so the latest wave of attacks should sharply reduce transits, and the war most likely continues beyond the next month with oil probably going much higher.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Expect Gulf export volumes to fall near term, supportive for crude.

insights.claim: The Saudi East-West pipeline narrative flip-flops: first touted as the Hormuz bypass, then dismissed after the Houthis took control of Bab el-Mandeb and hit the pipeline and Yanbu, now cited again as a reason to sell oil despite reduced flow rates.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Red Sea and bypass routes are also contested, limiting Gulf supply workarounds.

themes.theme: Refining squeeze: Russia, China and margin mean-reversion

insights.claim: Refining margins are extraordinary: over $100 per barrel for diesel, similar for jet, and around $80-something for gasoline, versus a decade average near $20 (about $15 excluding the Russia-Ukraine war and COVID).
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Current cracks are 5-7x normal, an unsustainable level that should mean-revert.

insights.claim: Consumers are largely accepting diesel and gasoline at about $250 per barrel equivalent, effectively demonstrating price acceptance of roughly $200-230 crude oil.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Demand tolerance suggests crude has room to rise toward where products already trade.
insights.quote: we're seeing mostly acceptance of diesel and gasoline at $250 barrel equivalents

insights.claim: The product squeeze stems mainly from Ukrainian strikes turning Russia from a massive diesel exporter into a diesel importer, plus China cutting refined product exports almost immediately after the US-Iran war began in March.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Product tightness is policy- and war-driven, so it can reverse quickly if those drivers change.

insights.claim: US and Canadian refiners normally run about 80% utilization in this seasonal period, which Young views as oligopolistic supply control; under a DOJ investigation and huge margins they are running about 95-96%, adding roughly a couple million barrels a day of products.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Extra refinery runs raise crude demand while easing product prices.

insights.claim: If Ukraine redirects strikes from Russian refineries to Russian oil exports, under pressure from Europe, refining margins could fall sharply, producing lower pump prices but higher crude prices as more crude is consumed.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Positioning implication: long crude producers, short refiners - the crack-to-crude rotation.

insights.claim: Cutting fuel taxes is a highly effective short-term fix for pump prices because gasoline and diesel demand is very price-insensitive, effectively shifting the pain to other countries; more fuel tax waivers may appear before the November midterms.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Pre-election tax waivers could lower pump prices without loosening crude.

themes.theme: Macro and cycle: Project Zimbabwe and underinvestment

insights.claim: Young uses the 'Project Zimbabwe' framework from his friend Harris Kupperman (transcribed 'Copperman'): debt service and structural spending force inflation and much higher commodity prices.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally inflationary backdrop favoring hard assets including oil.

insights.claim: Oil tends to follow gold and silver parabolic moves by 12 to 18 months; gold and silver went parabolic into early 2026 while oil has moved far less, implying substantial upside.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Precious metals' run is a lead indicator for an oil catch-up move.

insights.claim: Oil is mid-cycle after underinvestment since the 2012-2014 peak in exploration spend; Young expects higher prices then overinvestment over roughly the next three years leading eventually to oversupply, and would treat any recession as a buying opportunity before selling into the upcycle.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Defines a ~3-year bullish window with a planned exit into overinvestment.

insights.claim: The world must add roughly 6-12 million barrels a day of oil and NGL supply every year just to offset depletion, and rising shale share in US and Canada makes base decline rates rise, a 'Red Queen' effect.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Supply needs more conventional discovery and lower-tier shale development, neither of which is happening.

themes.theme: Positioning: short refiners and tankers, long small-cap E&Ps and onshore services

insights.claim: Young buys cheap out-of-the-money puts as 'TACO insurance' on indexes and susceptible companies he does not own, spending roughly 20 basis points to hedge against peace-headline gap-downs that could cost 10-20% in a month.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: A cheap convex hedge lets a fund stay long through jawboning-driven crashes like June.

insights.claim: Tankers and refiners - what has worked - look very risky: tanker rates face a big build cycle, and record refining margins are prompting restarts, expansions and new builds such as Dangote's planned Kenya refinery, so Young holds small net short exposure via derivatives.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Avoid or hedge with refiners and tankers; low P/Es there signal a cyclical top.

insights.claim: The most attractive opportunities are small-cap producers without refining exposure, many priced as if oil stays at $65-70 for a while.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Under-discounted producers offer leverage to higher crude and falling cracks.

insights.claim: Onshore oilfield services in the US, Canada and internationally are an underfollowed potential boom over the next 12-18 months, with some names trading at large discounts to replacement cost and double-digit free cash flow yields.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Onshore services are a less crowded alternative to the consensus offshore driller trade.

themes.theme: Natural gas oversupply and Europe's self-inflicted energy crisis

insights.claim: Young is avoiding US natural gas equities because commodity traders - Citadel via its vehicle (transcribed 'Apex') and a renamed Glencore-linked entity - are aggressively buying and drilling Haynesville assets, one deal citing 300 locations, and public producers lack the capital discipline refiners showed over the last decade.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Sustained gas drilling at low prices is not a recipe for higher gas prices despite LNG and data-center demand.

insights.claim: Europe's energy problems are largely self-induced by taxes, regulations and renewable mandates; Japan's approach of buying US gas fields and LNG project stakes will give its ratepayers LNG at a fraction of current prices for decades.
insights.speaker: Josh Young
insights.so_what: Upstream ownership deals are a model for energy security; Polish shale is unlikely to rescue Europe.
